entries.meaning: Very good at seeing or noticing small details. ---
examples: An eagle-eyed reader spotted the typo on page one.
The goalie was eagle-eyed all game.
The most eagle-eyed fans noticed the hidden clue in the trailer.

entries.meaning: Very serious and sincere, sometimes too serious. ---
examples: He's an earnest young man who wants to help.
They had a long, earnest conversation about the future.
Her second speech was more earnest and less funny.
entries.contrast: in earnest is a phrase: The work began in earnest (seriously, fully); Are you in earnest? (Do you really mean it?).

entries.meaning: Made of earth or baked clay. ---
examples: The old cabin had an earthen floor.
Engineers inspected the earthen dam after the flood.
Water was kept cool in large earthen jars.

entries.meaning: Earthly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He gave away all his earthly possessions.
Their earthly life was hard, but their faith was strong.
There's no earthly reason to wake up at five.
What earthly use is a phone without a battery?

senses.head: Relating to life in this world, not to heaven or the spirit
examples: He gave away all his earthly possessions.
Their earthly life was hard, but their faith was strong.

senses.head: After no, any or what: at all, possible
examples: There's no earthly reason to wake up at five.
What earthly use is a phone without a battery?

entries.meaning: Earthy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Mushrooms have an earthy flavor.
The room was decorated in warm, earthy colors.
This coffee is earthier than the Colombian one.
She has an earthy sense of humor.
His grandmother was a warm, earthy woman who laughed a lot.

senses.head: Tasting, smelling or looking like soil
examples: Mushrooms have an earthy flavor.
The room was decorated in warm, earthy colors.
This coffee is earthier than the Colombian one.

senses.head: Direct and natural, and not shy about the body or sex
examples: She has an earthy sense of humor.
His grandmother was a warm, earthy woman who laughed a lot.

entries.meaning: East has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They live on the east side of town.
Take the east exit from the parking garage.
We moved to the East Coast last year.
A cold east wind blew all day.
The east winds brought rain from the ocean.

senses.head: In, on or facing the east
examples: They live on the east side of town.
Take the east exit from the parking garage.
We moved to the East Coast last year.

senses.head: Of wind: blowing from the east
examples: A cold east wind blew all day.
The east winds brought rain from the ocean.

entries.contrast: In drive east it is an adverb, and in the East a noun. east is mostly for fixed names and parts: the East Coast, the east side; eastern is the general word: eastern Europe, eastern states.

entries.meaning: Of or from eastern Africa, such as Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia or Uganda. ---
examples: East African runners dominate long-distance races.
The restaurant serves East African food.
Swahili is spoken in many East African countries.

entries.meaning: Of or from the former German Democratic Republic. ---
examples: His parents escaped from East German territory in 1961.
East German athletes won many Olympic medals.
The car she drove was East German.
entries.contrast: Historical: the German Democratic Republic existed from 1949 to 1990. For the region today, say eastern German or in eastern Germany.

entries.meaning: Traveling or leading toward the east. ---
examples: There's a crash in the eastbound lanes of I-90.
The eastbound train leaves at 7:15.
Is this platform eastbound or westbound?

entries.meaning: Easterly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The ship sailed in an easterly direction.
Maine is the most easterly state in the country.
Strong easterly winds kept the boats in the harbor.
The forecast calls for light easterly breezes.

senses.head: Toward or in the east
examples: The ship sailed in an easterly direction.
Maine is the most easterly state in the country.

senses.head: Of wind: blowing from the east
examples: Strong easterly winds kept the boats in the harbor.
The forecast calls for light easterly breezes.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an easterly wind
entries.comparison: not gradable — but most easterly means 'farthest east'
entries.contrast: An easterly wind blows from the east, but an easterly direction is toward the east.

entries.meaning: Of the Orthodox Christian churches of Eastern Europe, Greece and the Middle East. ---
examples: Most of her family is Eastern Orthodox.
Eastern Orthodox Christians often celebrate Easter on a different date.
They were married in an Eastern Orthodox church in Chicago.
entries.contrast: In American English the Russian Church is usually called Russian Orthodox; Eastern Orthodox names the whole family of Orthodox churches. orthodox with a small o means 'traditional, accepted': orthodox methods.

entries.meaning: Farthest to the east. ---
examples: Lubec, Maine, is the easternmost town in the US.
We visited the easternmost point of the island.
The easternmost part of the state is mostly farmland.
entries.comparison: not gradable — it is already a superlative

entries.meaning: Moving or facing toward the east. ---
examples: The storm continued its eastward path.
Our eastward flight took only four hours.
The house has an eastward view of the mountains.
entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb: The storm moved eastward. eastwards with an s is more British.

entries.meaning: Relaxed and calm, not easily upset or worried. ---
examples: My new roommate is really easygoing.
He has an easygoing attitude about money.
She's much more easygoing than her sister.
entries.form: compound — easy + going; one word in American spelling

entries.meaning: Very cheerful, excited and full of energy. ---
examples: The coach was in an ebullient mood after the win.
She's an ebullient host who makes everyone feel welcome.
He was even more ebullient than usual at the reunion.

entries.meaning: Behaving or looking strange and unusual, often in a harmless or amusing way. ---
examples: My eccentric uncle keeps goats in his backyard.
Her fashion sense is a little eccentric.
He got more eccentric as he got older.
entries.contrast: an eccentric is also a noun: He's a lovable eccentric.

entries.meaning: Made up of many different styles, types or ideas. ---
examples: He has eclectic taste in music, from jazz to heavy metal.
The café is decorated in an eclectic mix of styles.
This year's lineup is more eclectic than ever.

entries.meaning: Not harmful to the environment. ---
examples: We switched to eco-friendly cleaning products.
Bamboo is more eco-friendly than plastic.
The new office was designed to be eco-friendly.
entries.contrast: friendly here means not harmful to, not kind. Environmentally friendly is the more formal version; green is the everyday one.

entries.meaning: Relating to the relationships between living things and their environment. ---
examples: The oil spill was an ecological disaster.
Scientists are studying the ecological impact of the new dam.
Wetlands have enormous ecological value.
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian экологичный or экологически чистый is eco-friendly, green or environmentally friendly in English: eco-friendly packaging, not ecological packaging. ecological means 'relating to nature and the environment': an ecological disaster.

entries.meaning: Of or from Ecuador, its people or its culture. ---
examples: We tried Ecuadorian ceviche in Queens.
Her father is Ecuadorian and her mother is Peruvian.
The Ecuadorian coast is famous for its bananas and shrimp.

entries.meaning: Ecumenical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The town held an ecumenical prayer service after the tragedy.
Leaders from several churches joined the ecumenical council.
The festival takes an ecumenical approach to music.
Her reading habits are wonderfully ecumenical.

senses.head: Bringing together different Christian churches or different religions
examples: The town held an ecumenical prayer service after the tragedy.
Leaders from several churches joined the ecumenical council.

senses.head: Including or accepting many different kinds of things
examples: The festival takes an ecumenical approach to music.
Her reading habits are wonderfully ecumenical.

entries.position: both — the religious sense mostly before a noun: an ecumenical service
entries.comparison: not gradable — but more ecumenical in the 'broad' sense

entries.meaning: Edgy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Everyone was edgy while we waited for the results.
Too much coffee makes me edgy.
The comedian is known for his edgy jokes.
The band's new album is edgier than their last one.

senses.head: Nervous, tense and easily annoyed
examples: Everyone was edgy while we waited for the results.
Too much coffee makes me edgy.

senses.head: Daring, modern and a little shocking
examples: The comedian is known for his edgy jokes.
The band's new album is edgier than their last one.

entries.meaning: Edible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Not all wild mushrooms are edible.
The flowers on the cake are edible.
We learned to find edible plants in the woods.
The cafeteria food was barely edible.
With some salt, the soup was at least edible.

senses.head: Safe to eat
examples: Not all wild mushrooms are edible.
The flowers on the cake are edible.
We learned to find edible plants in the woods.

senses.head: Good enough to eat, though not very good
examples: The cafeteria food was barely edible.
With some salt, the soup was at least edible.

entries.comparison: not gradable — but barely edible, more edible when it means 'good enough to eat'
entries.contrast: edibles is a plural noun, in American English often 'food containing cannabis'.

entries.meaning: Editorial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She joined the magazine's editorial staff.
The paper insists on its editorial independence.
The editorial page supported the mayor.
He draws editorial cartoons for a local paper.

senses.head: Relating to editing or to the people who prepare a book, newspaper or magazine
examples: She joined the magazine's editorial staff.
The paper insists on its editorial independence.

senses.head: Giving an opinion rather than just reporting facts
examples: The editorial page supported the mayor.
He draws editorial cartoons for a local paper.

entries.contrast: an editorial is a noun: an article that gives a newspaper's opinion.

entries.meaning: Educated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's an educated woman who speaks three languages.
Voters in the suburbs tend to be more educated.
He was educated at a small college in Ohio.
I don't know the exact number, but I can make an educated guess.
Read the reviews so you can make an educated choice.

senses.head: Having had a good education and knowing a lot
examples: She's an educated woman who speaks three languages.
Voters in the suburbs tend to be more educated.
He was educated at a small college in Ohio.

senses.head: Of a guess or decision: based on some knowledge, so likely to be right
examples: I don't know the exact number, but I can make an educated guess.
Read the reviews so you can make an educated choice.

entries.comparison: more/most — more educated, most educated; also better educated, well-educated

entries.meaning: Educational has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The educational system needs more funding.
He works for an educational nonprofit.
The trip to the museum was really educational.
We try to buy educational toys for the kids.
The documentary was more educational than the textbook.

senses.head: Relating to education and schools
examples: The educational system needs more funding.
He works for an educational nonprofit.

senses.head: Teaching you something useful or interesting
examples: The trip to the museum was really educational.
We try to buy educational toys for the kids.
The documentary was more educational than the textbook.

entries.position: both — the 'relating to education' sense only before a noun: the educational system
entries.comparison: more/most — more educational, most educational, in the 'teaches you something' sense

entries.meaning: From the time of King Edward VII of Britain, 1901 to 1910, or in its style. ---
examples: They restored a beautiful Edwardian house.
The movie is set in Edwardian England.
The costumes in the play were Edwardian.

entries.meaning: Strange and frightening in a mysterious way. ---
examples: An eerie silence fell over the empty school.
It was eerie how much he looked like his late father.
The abandoned mall is eerier at night.

entries.meaning: Of a man: looking or behaving in a way thought to be typical of women. ---
examples: He was bullied at school for being effeminate.
Critics called the singer's style effeminate.
In the remake, the character is less effeminate and more serious.
entries.contrast: Used about men and usually disapproving or offensive. It is not a neutral word for feminine.

entries.meaning: Effervescent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has an effervescent personality.
The most effervescent guest at the party was my grandmother.
Drop the effervescent tablet into a glass of water.
The wine is light and slightly effervescent.

senses.head: Of a person: lively, cheerful and full of energy
examples: She has an effervescent personality.
The most effervescent guest at the party was my grandmother.

senses.head: Of a liquid: producing small bubbles of gas
examples: Drop the effervescent tablet into a glass of water.
The wine is light and slightly effervescent.

entries.meaning: Weak, too refined and lacking energy or strength. ---
examples: The novel mocks the effete aristocrats of old Europe.
He dismissed his critics as effete intellectuals.
The new version sounds more effete than the original.
entries.contrast: A disapproving, bookish word; in American political talk it often mocks educated elites: effete snobs.

entries.meaning: Done so well that it seems to need no effort. ---
examples: She made the difficult dance look effortless.
He has an effortless style of writing.
Her piano playing grew more effortless every year.

entries.meaning: Showing strong feelings of praise, thanks or welcome, sometimes too much. ---
examples: The reviews of the play were effusive.
He gave me an effusive welcome at the door.
She was more effusive in her thanks than I expected.
entries.takes: in + noun: effusive in her praise

entries.meaning: Believing that all people are equal and should have the same rights and chances. ---
examples: They share the housework in a very egalitarian way.
The company has an egalitarian culture with no private offices.
The Nordic countries are among the most egalitarian in the world.

entries.meaning: Thinking only about yourself and not about other people. ---
examples: Toddlers are naturally egocentric.
He's an egocentric boss who never listens.
She became more egocentric after she got famous.

entries.meaning: Thinking you are better or more important than other people. ---
examples: He's so egotistical that he only talks about himself.
The egotistical star refused to share the stage.
She's the most egotistical person I've ever worked with.
entries.contrast: egotistical means 'thinking you are very important and talking about yourself'; selfish means 'caring only about your own needs'. Russian эгоистичный is usually selfish.

entries.meaning: Extremely bad and very obvious. ---
examples: It was an egregious error by the referee.
The company was fined for egregious safety violations.
This is the most egregious case of fraud the court has seen.

entries.meaning: Of or from Egypt, ancient or modern, its people or its culture. ---
examples: The museum has a large collection of ancient Egyptian art.
My doctor is Egyptian.
Egyptian cotton sheets are soft and expensive.

entries.meaning: Having many carefully planned parts or details. ---
examples: They planned an elaborate surprise party.
The dress had elaborate embroidery on the sleeves.
Each year the holiday decorations get more elaborate.
entries.contrast: The adjective ends in /ərət/; the verb to elaborate (give more details) ends in /əreɪt/: Can you ih-LAB-uh-rayt?

entries.meaning: Elastic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The pants have an elastic waistband.
Skin becomes less elastic with age.
This fabric is more elastic than cotton.
"Soon" is a very elastic word in this office.
Demand for gasoline is not very elastic.

senses.head: Able to stretch and then go back to its original shape
examples: The pants have an elastic waistband.
Skin becomes less elastic with age.
This fabric is more elastic than cotton.

senses.head: Able to change or be changed easily
examples: "Soon" is a very elastic word in this office.
Demand for gasoline is not very elastic.

entries.contrast: elastic is also a noun, the stretchy material: The elastic in these shorts is worn out.

entries.meaning: Extremely happy and excited. ---
examples: She was elated at the news of her promotion.
The elated fans ran onto the field.
I've never seen him more elated than on the day his son was born.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: We were elated
entries.takes: at, by or about + noun; to-infinitive; that-clause

entries.meaning: Chosen by voting. ---
examples: Elected officials should listen to voters.
The city has an elected school board.
She was the first elected female governor of the state.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the passive: She was elected mayor
entries.contrast: A person who has won but not yet started the job is -elect, after the noun: the president-elect, the governor-elect.

entries.meaning: Elective has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Hospitals postponed all elective surgery.
Art is an elective course at our high school.
Many insurers don't cover elective procedures.
She has never held elective office.
The governor is the highest elective position in the state.

senses.head: Chosen, not required; of medical treatment, planned rather than urgent
examples: Hospitals postponed all elective surgery.
Art is an elective course at our high school.
Many insurers don't cover elective procedures.

senses.head: Relating to an election or filled by an election
examples: She has never held elective office.
The governor is the highest elective position in the state.

entries.contrast: In American schools an elective is a noun, 'an optional class': I'm taking photography as an elective.

entries.meaning: Relating to elections or voting. ---
examples: The candidate needs 270 votes in the Electoral College.
Some states are changing their electoral maps.
There was no evidence of electoral fraud.

entries.meaning: Very exciting. ---
examples: The band gave an electrifying performance.
The atmosphere in the stadium was electrifying.
It was the most electrifying finish in years.

entries.meaning: Relating to electricity and magnetism together. ---
examples: Light is a form of electromagnetic radiation.
The device creates a strong electromagnetic field.
Radio waves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

entries.meaning: Electronic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Please turn off all electronic devices during takeoff.
The store sells electronic equipment and appliances.
We accept electronic payments only.
Doctors now keep electronic medical records.
The music is fully electronic, with no live instruments.

senses.head: Using microchips, transistors or other parts that control electric current
examples: Please turn off all electronic devices during takeoff.
The store sells electronic equipment and appliances.

senses.head: Done, sent or stored using computers
examples: We accept electronic payments only.
Doctors now keep electronic medical records.
The music is fully electronic, with no live instruments.

entries.contrast: electronic devices use microchips and circuits (a phone, a computer); electric things simply run on electricity (an electric fan, an electric car); electrical describes the system or work (electrical wiring, an electrical engineer).

entries.meaning: Elegant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She wore an elegant black dress.
The hotel lobby is simple but elegant.
The new design is more elegant than the old one.
It's an elegant solution to a difficult problem.
The proof is short and elegant.

senses.head: Graceful, attractive and stylish
examples: She wore an elegant black dress.
The hotel lobby is simple but elegant.
The new design is more elegant than the old one.

senses.head: Of an idea or solution: clever and simple
examples: It's an elegant solution to a difficult problem.
The proof is short and elegant.

entries.meaning: Elemental has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The storm showed the elemental power of the sea.
Fear of the dark is one of the most elemental human fears.
Diamonds are made of elemental carbon.
Elemental sodium reacts violently with water.

senses.head: Basic and powerful, like the forces of nature
examples: The storm showed the elemental power of the sea.
Fear of the dark is one of the most elemental human fears.

senses.head: In chemistry: in the form of a pure chemical element
examples: Diamonds are made of elemental carbon.
Elemental sodium reacts violently with water.

entries.position: both — the chemistry sense only before a noun: elemental carbon
entries.contrast: Not the same as elementary (basic, simple): an elementary mistake, but elemental forces of nature.

entries.meaning: Elementary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He made an elementary mistake in the math.
The questions were fairly elementary.
Let's start with the most elementary rules of grammar.
My daughter is in elementary school.
He's been an elementary teacher for twenty years.

senses.head: Basic and simple
examples: He made an elementary mistake in the math.
The questions were fairly elementary.
Let's start with the most elementary rules of grammar.

senses.head: Relating to the first stage of school, for children aged about 5 to 11
examples: My daughter is in elementary school.
He's been an elementary teacher for twenty years.

entries.position: both — the school sense only before a noun: elementary school
entries.comparison: more/most — more elementary, most elementary, in the 'basic' sense

entries.meaning: Elevated has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The test showed elevated levels of lead in the water.
Her blood pressure was slightly elevated.
Chicago's elevated trains are called the L.
The house sits on an elevated site above the river.
The speech was written in elevated language.
Her tone became more elevated when the cameras were on.

senses.head: Higher than normal in level or amount
examples: The test showed elevated levels of lead in the water.
Her blood pressure was slightly elevated.

senses.head: Raised above the ground
examples: Chicago's elevated trains are called the L.
The house sits on an elevated site above the river.

senses.head: Formal, serious or high in rank or style
examples: The speech was written in elevated language.
Her tone became more elevated when the cameras were on.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the best, most skilled or most powerful group. ---
examples: She trained with elite athletes before the Olympics.
He was a member of an elite military unit.
It's one of the most elite colleges in the country.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an elite school
entries.contrast: the elite is a noun, the most powerful or talented group. elitist is the disapproving word for a person or attitude that looks down on ordinary people.

entries.meaning: From the time of Queen Elizabeth I of England, or in its style. ---
examples: We're studying Elizabethan drama this semester.
The actors wore Elizabethan costumes.
The manor house is Elizabethan, built in 1580.
entries.contrast: It refers to Queen Elizabeth I (1558–1603), the age of Shakespeare, not to Elizabeth II.

entries.meaning: Elliptical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The earth moves around the sun in an elliptical orbit.
They bought an elliptical dining table for the narrow room.
His answer was short and elliptical.
Her later poems are even more elliptical than her early ones.

senses.head: Shaped like a flattened circle; oval
examples: The earth moves around the sun in an elliptical orbit.
They bought an elliptical dining table for the narrow room.

senses.head: Of speech or writing, leaving out words or details, so that it is hard to understand
examples: His answer was short and elliptical.
Her later poems are even more elliptical than her early ones.

entries.comparison: more/most — more elliptical (the 'unclear' sense); the shape sense is not gradable
entries.contrast: an elliptical (noun) is an exercise machine at the gym.

entries.meaning: Longer and thinner than usual. ---
examples: The figures in his paintings have elongated faces.
The shadows grew elongated as the sun went down.
The new model has a more elongated shape than the old one.

entries.meaning: Eloquent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She gave an eloquent speech at her father's funeral.
He is one of the most eloquent writers of his generation.
The senator was eloquent on the subject of health care.
Her silence was an eloquent answer.
The empty seats were eloquent proof that the show had failed.

senses.head: Speaking or writing well, in a way that is clear and moving
examples: She gave an eloquent speech at her father's funeral.
He is one of the most eloquent writers of his generation.
The senator was eloquent on the subject of health care.

senses.head: Showing a feeling or meaning clearly without words
examples: Her silence was an eloquent answer.
The empty seats were eloquent proof that the show had failed.

entries.meaning: Hard to find, catch, achieve or describe. ---
examples: The team is still chasing that elusive first championship.
Snow leopards are among the most elusive animals in the world.
A good night's sleep has been elusive since the baby was born.

entries.meaning: Extremely thin and weak because of illness or lack of food. ---
examples: Rescuers found an emaciated dog tied up behind the house.
After months in the hospital, he looked pale and emaciated.
The horses were more emaciated than anyone had expected.

entries.meaning: Embattled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The embattled mayor refused to resign.
The company is more embattled now than it was a year ago.
Teachers at the embattled school say they need more support.
Supplies were flown into the embattled city.
The embattled troops held out for three weeks.

senses.head: Facing a lot of criticism or serious problems
body: (находящийся под огнём критики, в трудном положении)
examples: The embattled mayor refused to resign.
The company is more embattled now than it was a year ago.
Teachers at the embattled school say they need more support.

senses.head: Of a place or army, surrounded by enemies in a war
examples: Supplies were flown into the embattled city.
The embattled troops held out for three weeks.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: the embattled CEO

entries.meaning: Embedded has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The doctor removed a piece of glass embedded in his foot.
Fossils are embedded in the rock.
Racism was deeply embedded in the town's history.
These habits are so embedded that they are hard to change.
The car's embedded software controls the brakes.
You can play the embedded video right on the page.
An embedded reporter traveled with the unit.

senses.head: Fixed firmly inside something solid
examples: The doctor removed a piece of glass embedded in his foot.
Fossils are embedded in the rock.

senses.head: Forming a deep, lasting part of a culture, mind or group
examples: Racism was deeply embedded in the town's history.
These habits are so embedded that they are hard to change.

senses.head: Built into a larger system or device, or placed inside a group to work with it
examples: The car's embedded software controls the brakes.
You can play the embedded video right on the page.
An embedded reporter traveled with the unit.

entries.comparison: not gradable — degree with deeply or firmly: deeply embedded

entries.meaning: Typical of something and serving as a symbol of it. ---
examples: The long lines at the DMV are emblematic of the problem.
The Golden Gate Bridge is the most emblematic sight in San Francisco.
His story is emblematic of a whole generation of immigrants.

entries.meaning: Feeling braver or more confident, usually because of something that has happened. ---
examples: Emboldened by the first win, the team started taking more risks.
She felt emboldened to ask for a raise.
After the vote, the protesters were more emboldened than ever.

entries.meaning: Having a raised design or letters pressed into the surface. ---
examples: The wedding invitations were printed on embossed paper.
The leather notebook is embossed with her initials.
Run your finger over the embossed numbers on the card.

entries.meaning: Deeply involved in an argument, conflict or difficult situation. ---
examples: The senator is embroiled in a campaign finance scandal.
They became embroiled in a bitter fight over the will.
The longer the war lasted, the more embroiled the country became.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb or after the noun: a company embroiled in a lawsuit

entries.meaning: Embryonic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The plan is still in its embryonic stage.
In 1995 the online shopping industry was embryonic.
The lab studies embryonic stem cells.
The scan showed normal embryonic growth.

senses.head: At a very early stage of development
examples: The plan is still in its embryonic stage.
In 1995 the online shopping industry was embryonic.

senses.head: Relating to an embryo
examples: The lab studies embryonic stem cells.
The scan showed normal embryonic growth.

entries.position: both — the biology sense only before a noun: embryonic cells

entries.meaning: Starting to exist, develop or become known. ---
examples: The fund invests in emerging markets such as India and Brazil.
The festival showcases emerging artists.
Doctors are worried about an emerging strain of the virus.
entries.position: attributive only — The truth is emerging is the verb

entries.meaning: Retired but allowed to keep a title, especially at a university. ---
examples: He is a professor emeritus of history at Yale.
The emeritus pastor still preaches on holidays.
She became president emeritus when she stepped down.
entries.position: after the noun — usually: professor emeritus; also before: emeritus professor
entries.contrast: It does not simply mean 'honorary': an emeritus professor really held the job and has retired, keeping the title.

entries.meaning: Famous and respected, especially in a profession. ---
examples: The panel included several eminent scientists.
She was one of the most eminent surgeons in the country.
Her grandfather was an eminent judge.
entries.contrast: Not imminent (about to happen): an eminent scientist, but an imminent storm.

entries.meaning: Emotional has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Her friends gave her a lot of emotional support.
The divorce took an emotional toll on the kids.
He got very emotional when he talked about his mother.
I'm more emotional than my husband.
It was an emotional reunion at the airport.
Abortion is a highly emotional issue.

senses.head: Relating to feelings
examples: Her friends gave her a lot of emotional support.
The divorce took an emotional toll on the kids.

senses.head: Showing strong feelings, or easily showing them
examples: He got very emotional when he talked about his mother.
I'm more emotional than my husband.

senses.head: Causing strong feelings
examples: It was an emotional reunion at the airport.
Abortion is a highly emotional issue.

entries.meaning: Showing no feelings. ---
examples: The defendant stared ahead with an emotionless face.
Her voice was flat and emotionless.
The robot sounded more emotionless than I expected.

entries.meaning: Causing strong feelings. ---
examples: Gun control is a very emotive issue.
The ad uses emotive language to get donations.
Her second speech was even more emotive than the first.
entries.contrast: emotive describes words and issues that stir feelings; a person who shows feelings is emotional, not emotive.

entries.meaning: Able to understand and share other people's feelings. ---
examples: She's a very empathetic nurse.

Worry was etched into his face.

Nothing in this world is eternal.

Every doctor here signs an ethical code.

entries.meaning: From Ethiopia, or belonging to its people and culture. ---

entries.meaning: Feeling or showing very great happiness and excitement. ---
examples: The fans were euphoric after the win.

entries.meaning: Eurasian has 2 distinct senses.

Her mother is Eurasian.

The port city had a large Eurasian community.

entries.meaning: Treating Europe and its culture as the center of everything. ---

The museum is rewriting its Eurocentric labels.

entries.meaning: Evangelical has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Belonging to the Protestant churches that stress the Bible and personal conversion
examples: She was raised in an evangelical church in Texas.
Evangelical voters were a large part of the turnout.

senses.head: Trying eagerly to convince other people of a belief
examples: He is evangelical about cold showers.
The company has an almost evangelical faith in its own product.

entries.comparison: more/most — more evangelical, most evangelical (the 'zealous' sense)

entries.meaning: Made thicker by having most of the water removed. ---
examples: The recipe calls for a can of evaporated milk.

You can substitute cream for evaporated milk in a pinch.

She got more evasive the longer we talked.

senses.head: Meant to get out of the way of danger
examples: The pilot took evasive action.
The deer made an evasive jump into the trees.

entries.meaning: Even has 4 distinct senses.

senses.head: Flat, level and smooth

The new concrete is much more even than the old walkway.

You bought lunch, so now we're even.

Keep the oven at an even temperature.

entries.comparison: more/most — more even, most even (the 'level' and 'steady' senses)

entries.meaning: Treating everyone fairly and in the same way. ---

entries.meaning: Calm by nature and not easily made angry. ---
examples: He is an even-tempered man who rarely raises his voice.
Golden retrievers are usually even-tempered.
She is more even-tempered than anyone else on the team.

entries.meaning: Treating both sides fairly and equally. ---

entries.contrast: Also written even-handed.

entries.meaning: Full of interesting or important things happening. ---

entries.meaning: Always becoming different, never staying the same. ---

entries.meaning: Always there, and never going away. ---

senses.head: Staying useful or popular no matter how much time passes

entries.meaning: Lasting forever, or seeming to. ---
examples: The hymn promises everlasting life.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: everlasting life

Spanish is her everyday language at home.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: everyday life

entries.meaning: Built on research and proof rather than on opinion or habit. ---
examples: The clinic uses only evidence-based treatments.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: evidence-based medicine

senses.head: Deeply bad in a moral way, and wanting to harm others
examples: He plays the evil wizard in the new movie.
No one is born evil.
She is the most evil character in the whole series.

senses.head: Very unpleasant, especially to the nose
examples: An evil smell came from the basement.
He gave me an evil look and walked out.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — eviler or more evil, evilest or most evil

entries.meaning: Bringing strong pictures, memories or feelings to mind. ---

senses.head: Happening by small steps rather than all at once
examples: The new phone is evolutionary, not revolutionary.
They favor an evolutionary approach to reform.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: evolutionary biology

entries.meaning: Holding a position automatically because of another job you hold. ---

entries.position: both — before a noun, or right after it: a member ex officio

entries.meaning: Completely correct and with no error in the details. ---

Her figures are more exact than the ones in the first report.

entries.meaning: Making someone very annoyed. ---

examples: Most of the difference is explainable by the weather.

Researchers want explainable software, not a black box.

entries.meaning: Meant to make something clearer or easier to understand. ---
examples: See the explanatory note at the bottom of the page.
The manual comes with explanatory diagrams.
A short explanatory video walks you through the form.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: an explanatory note
entries.contrast: Note the spelling: explain loses its i — explanatory, explanation.

entries.meaning: Explicit has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He gave explicit instructions not to be disturbed.
She was explicit about what she wanted.
Let me be more explicit: the answer is no.
The album carries an explicit lyrics warning.
Some scenes are sexually explicit.

senses.head: Said clearly and in detail, leaving no room for doubt
examples: He gave explicit instructions not to be disturbed.
She was explicit about what she wanted.
Let me be more explicit: the answer is no.

senses.head: Showing sex or violence openly
examples: The album carries an explicit lyrics warning.
Some scenes are sexually explicit.

entries.meaning: Exploding has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The movie ends with an exploding helicopter.
Exploding fireworks lit up the harbor.
The city is struggling with an exploding population.
Exploding demand caught the factory off guard.

senses.head: Blowing apart with great force
examples: The movie ends with an exploding helicopter.
Exploding fireworks lit up the harbor.

senses.head: Growing very fast in number or size
examples: The city is struggling with an exploding population.
Exploding demand caught the factory off guard.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the exploding population

entries.meaning: Treating people unfairly in order to profit from them. ---
examples: The report describes exploitative labor practices.
Those interest rates are plainly exploitative.
The second contract was even more exploitative than the first.

entries.meaning: Used unfairly for someone else's profit. ---
examples: Exploited farm workers often have no legal protection.
Interns felt exploited and quit.
She writes about exploited garment workers in Los Angeles.

entries.meaning: Done in order to find out more, before anything is decided. ---
examples: The two sides held exploratory talks in Geneva.
The surgeon ordered exploratory surgery.
She formed an exploratory committee for a Senate run.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: exploratory talks

entries.meaning: Explosive has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Dogs are trained to sniff out explosive material.
The gas is highly explosive.
The testimony was explosive.
Race and money are the most explosive topics on the council.
The company saw explosive growth in its first year.
He's an explosive runner off the line.

senses.head: Able to blow up
examples: Dogs are trained to sniff out explosive material.
The gas is highly explosive.

senses.head: Likely to cause sudden anger, argument or trouble
examples: The testimony was explosive.
Race and money are the most explosive topics on the council.

senses.head: Sudden, fast and powerful
examples: The company saw explosive growth in its first year.
He's an explosive runner off the line.

entries.contrast: Explosives is also a plural noun — the material itself.

entries.meaning: Growing faster and faster, by a larger amount each time. ---
examples: The chart shows exponential growth in users.
Costs rose at an exponential rate.
There's been an exponential increase in applications.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: exponential growth
entries.contrast: In math it is exact; in the newspaper it just means "very fast."

entries.meaning: Exposed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cabin sits on an exposed ridge.
Don't leave exposed wires where kids can reach them.
The north side of the house is more exposed to wind.
Workers were exposed to asbestos for years.
Anyone exposed to the virus should stay home.

senses.head: Not covered or protected from weather, danger or view
examples: The cabin sits on an exposed ridge.
Don't leave exposed wires where kids can reach them.
The north side of the house is more exposed to wind.

senses.head: Put in contact with something harmful
examples: Workers were exposed to asbestos for years.
Anyone exposed to the virus should stay home.

entries.meaning: Explaining facts or ideas rather than telling a story or arguing. ---
examples: The class teaches expository writing.
He cut the long expository passages from the script.
The first chapter is purely expository.

entries.meaning: Express has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Take the express train to Penn Station.
Ten items or fewer in the express lane.
Send it express mail if it has to be there Monday.
He came for the express purpose of apologizing.
You need her express permission in writing.

senses.head: Fast, and stopping at few places or handled ahead of the rest
examples: Take the express train to Penn Station.
Ten items or fewer in the express lane.
Send it express mail if it has to be there Monday.

senses.head: Stated clearly and on purpose
examples: He came for the express purpose of apologizing.
You need her express permission in writing.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: an express train
entries.contrast: Express is also a common verb (express an opinion) and a noun (take the express). The adjective only goes before a noun.

entries.meaning: Showing no feeling on the face or in the voice. ---
examples: Her face stayed expressionless through the whole verdict.
He answered in a flat, expressionless voice.
The guard was completely expressionless.
entries.comparison: not gradable — degree with completely: completely expressionless

entries.meaning: Showing thoughts and feelings clearly. ---
examples: The baby has big, expressive eyes.
His playing is technically fine but not very expressive.
She is more expressive in her second language than in her first.

entries.meaning: Exquisite has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She wore an exquisite silk dress.
The carving on the door is exquisite.
It was the most exquisite meal we had all year.
He has an exquisite sense of timing.
Waiting for the results was exquisite torture.

senses.head: Extremely beautiful and delicately made
examples: She wore an exquisite silk dress.
The carving on the door is exquisite.
It was the most exquisite meal we had all year.

senses.head: Of a feeling, very strong and finely felt
examples: He has an exquisite sense of timing.
Waiting for the results was exquisite torture.

entries.meaning: Still existing, especially after a long time. ---
examples: Only three extant copies of the map are known.
The oldest extant building in town dates to 1789.
Few of his letters are still extant.
entries.contrast: Not extinct, its near-opposite: extant species are the ones still alive.

entries.meaning: Spoken or done without preparation, made up as you go. ---
examples: She gave an extemporaneous speech at the reception.
His remarks were entirely extemporaneous.
The debate tournament has an extemporaneous round.
entries.contrast: Formal. Everyday English says off the cuff.

entries.meaning: Able to be made longer in size or in time. ---
examples: The ladder is extendable to twenty feet.
The lease is extendable for another two years.
It comes with an extendable handle.
entries.contrast: Also spelled extendible, but extendable is the usual American form.

entries.meaning: Extended has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He took an extended leave after the surgery.
The store has extended hours during the holidays.
Her extended family gathers every Thanksgiving.
The DVD has an extended version with twenty more minutes.

senses.head: Longer than usual or than planned
examples: He took an extended leave after the surgery.
The store has extended hours during the holidays.

senses.head: Including more than the usual core
examples: Her extended family gathers every Thanksgiving.
The DVD has an extended version with twenty more minutes.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: an extended stay
entries.contrast: Extended family means aunts, cousins and grandparents — not a big family.

entries.meaning: Covering a large area or a lot of material. ---
examples: She has extensive experience in public health.
The library's collection is extensive.
The damage was more extensive than the first reports suggested.
entries.contrast: Extensive is about how much ground it covers; intensive is about how concentrated the effort is.

entries.meaning: Making an offense seem less serious by explaining why it happened. ---
examples: The judge found extenuating circumstances and reduced the sentence.
We can waive the fee if there are extenuating circumstances.
There were extenuating factors the report never mentioned.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun, almost always circumstances
entries.contrast: It lives in one phrase: extenuating circumstances. You will rarely meet it anywhere else.

entries.meaning: On or forming the outside of something, especially a building. ---
examples: The exterior walls need paint.
Use exterior latex for the trim.
They shot the exterior scenes in Toronto.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: exterior walls
entries.contrast: Exterior is the outside surface of a thing (a house, a car); external is the wider word for anything outside (external pressure, external hard drive).

entries.meaning: External has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The label says "for external use only."
I back everything up to an external drive.
The board hired an external auditor.
The pressure was external, not from anyone on the team.

senses.head: On the outside, or coming from outside
examples: The label says "for external use only."
I back everything up to an external drive.

senses.head: Belonging to something outside the group or organization
examples: The board hired an external auditor.
The pressure was external, not from anyone on the team.

entries.meaning: Extinct has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The passenger pigeon has been extinct since 1914.
Several frog species have gone extinct in the last decade.
Pay phones are all but extinct.
The island sits on an extinct volcano.
Geologists say the crater is extinct, not dormant.

senses.head: No longer existing, of a species or a way of life
examples: The passenger pigeon has been extinct since 1914.
Several frog species have gone extinct in the last decade.
Pay phones are all but extinct.

senses.head: Of a volcano, no longer active and not expected to erupt again
examples: The island sits on an extinct volcano.
Geologists say the crater is extinct, not dormant.

entries.comparison: not gradable — a species either is or isn't
entries.contrast: Extinct (died out) and extinguished (put out, of a fire) come from the same root but are not interchangeable.

entries.meaning: Of a price or rate, so high that it feels like robbery. ---
examples: The airport charges extortionate parking rates.
Payday lenders charge extortionate interest.
Their fee is more extortionate than anything I've seen.

entries.meaning: More than the usual or expected number or amount. ---
examples: Bring an extra pair of socks.
Guacamole is extra.
She worked extra hours all through December.
entries.contrast: Extra is also an adverb (extra large, extra carefully) and a noun (an extra in a movie). Note an extra chair, never a extra chair.

entries.meaning: Bigger than the large size. ---
examples: Do you have this shirt in extra-large?
He ordered an extra-large pizza for four people.
The recipe calls for two extra-large eggs.

entries.meaning: Done at school but outside regular classes. ---
examples: Colleges look at extracurricular activities too.
Band and debate are her main extracurricular interests.
Budget cuts hit the extracurricular programs first.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: extracurricular activities
entries.contrast: Jokingly used for an affair: his extracurricular activities.

entries.meaning: Done outside the courts and without their authority. ---
examples: The report documents extrajudicial killings.
The families reached an extrajudicial settlement.
Extrajudicial detention is banned under the treaty.

entries.meaning: Happening outside a marriage, with someone who is not your husband or wife. ---
examples: He admitted to an extramarital affair.
The book studies extramarital relationships across cultures.
Rumors of an extramarital romance ended his campaign.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: an extramarital affair

entries.meaning: Not connected with what is being dealt with, and therefore unnecessary. ---
examples: Cut the extraneous detail from the introduction.
That argument is extraneous to the case.
Extraneous noise ruined the recording.
entries.русский: посторонний, лишний, не относящийся к делу

entries.meaning: Extraordinary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has an extraordinary memory for names.
What he did that night was extraordinary.
It was the most extraordinary thing I've ever seen.
The board called an extraordinary meeting.
The envoy is an ambassador extraordinary.

senses.head: Far beyond what is usual, in a way that surprises or impresses
examples: She has an extraordinary memory for names.
What he did that night was extraordinary.
It was the most extraordinary thing I've ever seen.

senses.head: Arranged for a special purpose, outside the normal schedule
examples: The board called an extraordinary meeting.
The envoy is an ambassador extraordinary.

entries.contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the a of extra almost disappears: ik-STROR-duh-ner-ee, not "extra-ordinary."

entries.meaning: Coming from outside the five normal senses. ---
examples: The lab tested claims of extrasensory perception.
She says she has some kind of extrasensory ability.
There is no solid evidence for extrasensory powers.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun, nearly always perception

entries.meaning: Coming from, or existing, outside the earth. ---
examples: They scan the sky for extraterrestrial signals.
No extraterrestrial life has ever been found.
The rock turned out to be extraterrestrial in origin.
entries.contrast: Also a noun, shortened to ET: the search for extraterrestrials.

entries.meaning: Extreme has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He was in extreme pain.
Use it only in an extreme emergency.
This winter was more extreme than any in living memory.
He holds extreme political views.
That's an extreme position, even for him.
She's into extreme sports — base jumping, mostly.
The channel shows extreme skiing all winter.

senses.head: Very great in degree, far beyond the normal
examples: He was in extreme pain.
Use it only in an extreme emergency.
This winter was more extreme than any in living memory.

senses.head: Of opinions, far from what most people think, and often dangerous
examples: He holds extreme political views.
That's an extreme position, even for him.

senses.head: Of sports, dangerous and exciting
examples: She's into extreme sports — base jumping, mostly.
The channel shows extreme skiing all winter.

entries.contrast: Extremes is also a noun: go to extremes, the extremes of the desert.

entries.meaning: Holding political or religious views far outside the mainstream, often with violence. ---
examples: The site was taken down for hosting extremist content.
He was drawn into an extremist group online.
Extremist violence rose sharply that year.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: extremist groups
entries.contrast: An extremist is also a noun, and the commoner use: the group was founded by extremists.

entries.meaning: Coming from outside a person or thing, not part of its basic nature. ---
examples: Grades and money are extrinsic rewards; curiosity is an intrinsic one.
The value of a dollar bill is extrinsic — the paper itself is worth almost nothing.
Researchers looked at both genetic and extrinsic factors.

entries.meaning: Outgoing and full of energy around other people; enjoying company. ---
examples: She's very extroverted and loves meeting new people.
My extroverted brother talks to everyone on the bus.
I'm more extroverted at work than I am at home.
entries.form: -ed from extrovert; psychologists also spell it extraverted

entries.meaning: Exuberant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The exuberant fans poured onto the field.
The kids were exuberant on the last day of school.
Her exuberant laugh filled the room.
The garden was a mass of exuberant green.
The painting uses exuberant reds and yellows.

senses.head: Full of energy, excitement and happiness
examples: The exuberant fans poured onto the field.
The kids were exuberant on the last day of school.
Her exuberant laugh filled the room.

senses.head: Growing thickly and strongly, or bright and full of life in style
examples: The garden was a mass of exuberant green.
The painting uses exuberant reds and yellows.

entries.meaning: Attractive or unusual enough to make people notice it. ---
examples: The store needs an eye-catching sign.
Her red coat was very eye-catching.
Which of these two designs is more eye-catching?

entries.meaning: So large, surprising or striking that it makes you stare — informal. ---
examples: The house sold for an eye-popping $4 million.
The special effects were eye-popping.
The team put up eye-popping numbers this season.

entries.meaning: Famous and talked about a lot, often in stories that may not be completely true. ---
examples: We finally drove the fabled Route 66.

The city is fabled for its jazz clubs.

entries.meaning: Invented in order to deceive people; not true. ---
examples: The reporter was fired for publishing fabricated quotes.
His lawyers say the evidence was fabricated.
She told a completely fabricated story about her past.

entries.meaning: Fabulous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You look fabulous in that dress!

The view from the top was fabulous.
He made a fabulous fortune in oil.
The family lived in fabulous wealth.

senses.head: Extremely good; wonderful — informal
examples: You look fabulous in that dress!
We had a fabulous time in New Orleans.
The view from the top was fabulous.

senses.head: Unusually great in amount or size
examples: He made a fabulous fortune in oil.

entries.meaning: Helping someone avoid looking foolish or losing other people's respect. ---
examples: The two sides agreed on a face-saving compromise.
Resigning was a face-saving move for the senator.
They needed a face-saving way to end the strike.
entries.form: compound — from the phrase save face

entries.meaning: With the people physically together in the same place, not by phone or online. ---
examples: I'd rather have a face-to-face conversation about this.
Classes will be face-to-face again this fall.
Nothing replaces face-to-face contact with customers.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: a face-to-face meeting
entries.contrast: After a verb it is often the adverb, usually written open: We finally met face to face.

entries.meaning: Having no individual character; impersonal and unknown. ---
examples: I'm tired of dealing with faceless bureaucrats.

Big corporations can seem faceless and cold.

entries.meaning: Joking about something serious, or not meaning what you say to be taken seriously. ---

I was being facetious when I said I'd quit.
He made a facetious comment about the funeral.

entries.meaning: Of or on the face. ---
examples: His facial expression didn't change.
The phone uses facial recognition to unlock.
He has a lot of facial hair.
entries.contrast: A facial is also a noun: a beauty treatment for the face.

entries.meaning: Facile has 2 distinct senses.
examples: That's a facile explanation for a complicated problem.
Critics called the book's conclusions facile.
There are no facile solutions to poverty.
The Yankees won a facile victory.
He's a facile writer who can turn out a column in an hour.

senses.head: Too simple; not showing careful thought
examples: That's a facile explanation for a complicated problem.
Critics called the book's conclusions facile.
There are no facile solutions to poverty.

senses.head: Done with little effort; smooth and fluent, sometimes too much so
examples: The Yankees won a facile victory.
He's a facile writer who can turn out a column in an hour.

entries.contrast: Usually not a compliment: it does not simply mean 'easy' (лёгкий). A facile answer is too simple to be taken seriously.

entries.meaning: Done to find out the facts about a situation. ---
examples: The senator went on a fact-finding trip to the border.
A fact-finding committee will look into the accident.
The first meeting is a fact-finding session.

entries.meaning: Made by machines in a factory, not by hand or at home. ---

entries.meaning: Based on facts or containing facts, not opinions. ---

Please keep your answers short and factual.
The second article was more factual and less emotional.
entries.contrast: Russian фактический often means actual or real: фактическая стоимость is the actual cost. English factual means only 'based on facts' or 'about facts': a factual report, a factual error.

entries.meaning: Faded has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Having lost its color or brightness
examples: He wore an old pair of faded jeans.
The sign on the barn was faded and hard to read.
The photo was more faded than I remembered.

senses.head: No longer strong, famous or clear
examples: She's a faded movie star living in Palm Springs.
I have only faded memories of that house.

entries.meaning: Measured on the temperature scale on which water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212. ---
examples: It was 95 degrees Fahrenheit in Phoenix today.
Bake at 350 degrees Fahrenheit for 25 minutes.
Most Americans only know the Fahrenheit scale.
entries.position: after the noun — after a number of degrees: 72 degrees Fahrenheit; also before a noun: the Fahrenheit scale
entries.contrast: Americans use Fahrenheit for weather, cooking and body temperature: 32°F is freezing and 98.6°F is normal body temperature. Always with a capital F.

entries.meaning: Designed to stay safe if something goes wrong; certain to work. ---
examples: The elevator has a fail-safe braking system.
There's no fail-safe way to pick stocks.
The system is supposed to be fail-safe.

entries.meaning: Failing has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She moved in with her daughter because of failing health.

Grandpa's failing eyesight means he can't drive anymore.

Anything below 60 counts as a failing score.

senses.head: Becoming weaker or worse
examples: She moved in with her daughter because of failing health.
In the failing light we couldn't see the trail.
Grandpa's failing eyesight means he can't drive anymore.

senses.head: Not successful; losing money, customers or support
examples: He took over a failing restaurant and turned it around.
The state stepped in to fix failing schools.

senses.head: Of a grade or score: too low to pass
examples: He got a failing grade in chemistry.
Anything below 60 counts as a failing score.

entries.position: attributive only — failing health; after be it is usually the verb: His health is failing
entries.contrast: A failing is also a noun, meaning a weakness: We all have our failings.

entries.meaning: Faint has 3 distinct senses.
examples: There was a faint smell of smoke in the hall.
The music grew fainter as we walked away.
I could see a faint light in the distance.
There's still a faint hope that they'll find survivors.
I don't have the faintest idea where he went.
She gave a faint smile.
I felt faint from the heat.
She was faint with hunger after the long hike.

senses.head: Hard to see, hear or smell; not strong
examples: There was a faint smell of smoke in the hall.
The music grew fainter as we walked away.
I could see a faint light in the distance.

senses.head: Very small; slight
examples: There's still a faint hope that they'll find survivors.
I don't have the faintest idea where he went.
She gave a faint smile.

senses.head: Feeling weak and dizzy, as if you are about to lose consciousness
examples: I felt faint from the heat.
She was faint with hunger after the long hike.

entries.русский: слабый, едва заметный; близкий к обмороку
entries.position: both — in the 'about to pass out' sense only after a verb: I feel faint
entries.contrast: I don't have the faintest idea means 'I have no idea at all'. Faint is also a verb, 'to lose consciousness' (She fainted). Feint (a fake move) sounds the same.

entries.meaning: Easily frightened and lacking the nerve to act. ---
examples: The hike along the ridge is not for the faint-hearted.
He was too faint-hearted to ask for a raise.
Faint-hearted investors sold everything that week.
entries.contrast: Very often in the fixed phrase not for the faint-hearted = not for people who scare easily.

entries.meaning: Lacking courage; easily frightened or discouraged. ---
examples: Fainthearted investors sold everything when prices fell.
Congress has been too fainthearted to raise taxes.
Don't be so fainthearted — just ask her out.
entries.form: compound — faint + heart + -ed; also spelled faint-hearted
entries.contrast: Most often met in not for the fainthearted (not for people who scare easily), where the fainthearted is a noun.

entries.meaning: Fair has 6 distinct senses.

We got a fair price for the car.
