The car is in fair shape for its age.
People with fair skin burn easily.
She has fairer hair than her sister.
The baby had fair curls.
The forecast is fair and sunny for the weekend.
We sailed out under fair skies.

senses.head: Treating people equally and according to the rules; just
examples: It's not fair that she gets more money for the same job.
The judge was strict but fair.
Everyone deserves a fair trial.

senses.head: Reasonable and acceptable in the circumstances
examples: We got a fair price for the car.
That's a fair question.
It's fair to say the plan didn't work.

senses.head: Fairly large in amount, number or distance
examples: It's a fair distance from here to the lake.
A fair number of people left early.

senses.head: Neither very good nor very bad; average
examples: His condition is only fair after the surgery.
The car is in fair shape for its age.

senses.head: Of hair or skin: light in color
examples: People with fair skin burn easily.
She has fairer hair than her sister.
The baby had fair curls.

senses.head: Of weather: pleasant and dry, without rain
examples: The forecast is fair and sunny for the weekend.
We sailed out under fair skies.

entries.position: both — in the 'fairly large' sense only before a noun: a fair number
entries.takes: to + person: It isn't fair to her; to-infinitive in it's fair to say
entries.contrast: Russian светлый about hair and skin is fair in a slightly formal style; everyday American English more often says blond hair and light or pale skin. A fair is a noun (the county fair), and in play fair the word is an adverb.

entries.meaning: Fair-haired has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A fair-haired girl answered the door.
Both boys are fair-haired like their dad.
He's the boss's fair-haired boy and gets every promotion.
For a few years she was the network's fair-haired girl.

senses.head: Having light-colored hair
examples: A fair-haired girl answered the door.
Both boys are fair-haired like their dad.

senses.head: Favored by someone in power — in fair-haired boy, informal American
examples: He's the boss's fair-haired boy and gets every promotion.
For a few years she was the network's fair-haired girl.

entries.position: both — in the 'favorite' sense only before a noun: the boss's fair-haired boy

entries.meaning: Judging people and situations fairly, without prejudice. ---
examples: We need a fair-minded person to settle this.
Most fair-minded voters would agree.
He's more fair-minded than most of his colleagues.

entries.meaning: Faithful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Max was a faithful dog who followed her everywhere.
She's been a faithful customer for twenty years.
He stayed faithful to his wife for fifty years.
The movie is faithful to the novel.
It's the most faithful translation I've read.

senses.head: Loyal; staying with a person, belief or group
examples: Max was a faithful dog who followed her everywhere.
She's been a faithful customer for twenty years.
He stayed faithful to his wife for fifty years.

senses.head: Accurate; true to the original
examples: The movie is faithful to the novel.
It's the most faithful translation I've read.

entries.takes: to + person, belief or original: faithful to his wife, faithful to the book
entries.contrast: About a husband, wife or partner, faithful means not having sex with anyone else, and unfaithful means cheating.

entries.meaning: Fake has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The police arrested him for using a fake ID.
Is that fur real or fake?
The site is full of fake reviews.
She gave me a big fake smile.
I can't stand him — he's so fake.
His Southern accent sounds fake.

senses.head: Made to look like something real, to trick people or to cost less
examples: The police arrested him for using a fake ID.
Is that fur real or fake?
The site is full of fake reviews.

senses.head: Pretended; not sincere
examples: She gave me a big fake smile.
I can't stand him — he's so fake.
His Southern accent sounds fake.

entries.comparison: not gradable — but about insincere people so fake and more fake are common in speech
entries.contrast: Fake vs false: fake is for copies made to fool people (fake money, a fake ID); false is for things that are not true (a false statement) and a few replacements (false teeth). Fake is also a verb (He faked an injury) and a noun (The painting is a fake).

entries.meaning: Based on a false idea or bad reasoning — formal. ---
examples: The argument is fallacious because it assumes what it tries to prove.
The ad makes several fallacious claims.
Critics called the report's reasoning fallacious.

entries.meaning: Fallen has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The yard was covered in fallen leaves.
A fallen tree blocked the road.
Memorial Day honors fallen soldiers.
The town built a monument to its fallen heroes.
The movie is about a fallen star trying to make a comeback.
The fallen dictator fled the country.

senses.head: Lying on the ground after falling
examples: The yard was covered in fallen leaves.
A fallen tree blocked the road.

senses.head: Killed in a war
examples: Memorial Day honors fallen soldiers.
The town built a monument to its fallen heroes.

senses.head: Having lost power, status or a good moral reputation
examples: The movie is about a fallen star trying to make a comeback.
The fallen dictator fled the country.

entries.contrast: The fallen is also a noun: soldiers killed in war.

entries.meaning: Able to make mistakes or be wrong. ---
examples: Doctors are human and fallible like everyone else.
Memory is fallible, so write it down.
Eyewitness testimony is more fallible than most juries think.

entries.meaning: Falling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Watch out for falling rocks.
He was hit by a falling branch.
A falling star streaked across the sky.
Falling prices are good news for shoppers.
The company is struggling with falling sales.

senses.head: Coming down toward the ground
examples: Watch out for falling rocks.
He was hit by a falling branch.
A falling star streaked across the sky.

senses.head: Going down in amount or level
examples: Falling prices are good news for shoppers.
The company is struggling with falling sales.

entries.position: attributive only — after be it is the verb: Prices are falling

entries.meaning: Fallow has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The farmer leaves one field fallow every year.
Weeds grew over the fallow land.
After his first hit, he went through a long fallow period.
The fallow years between albums were hard for the band.

senses.head: Of farmland: left without crops for a season so the soil can recover
examples: The farmer leaves one field fallow every year.
Weeds grew over the fallow land.

senses.head: Of a period of time: when little is done or produced
examples: After his first hit, he went through a long fallow period.
The fallow years between albums were hard for the band.

entries.position: both — often in lie fallow and leave fallow

entries.meaning: False has 4 distinct senses.
examples: The rumor turned out to be false.
True or false: the sun is a star.
He gave the police a false name.
It was a false alarm — there was no fire.
Don't give her false hope.
I had a false impression of him.
My grandfather has false teeth.
She wore false eyelashes to the party.
Spare me the false modesty.
Her cheerfulness sounded false.

senses.head: Not true or correct
examples: The rumor turned out to be false.
True or false: the sun is a star.
He gave the police a false name.

senses.head: Based on a mistake; wrong
examples: It was a false alarm — there was no fire.
Don't give her false hope.
I had a false impression of him.

senses.head: Not natural; artificial
examples: My grandfather has false teeth.
She wore false eyelashes to the party.

senses.head: Not sincere; pretended
examples: Spare me the false modesty.
Her cheerfulness sounded false.

entries.position: both — in the 'artificial' sense only before a noun: false teeth
entries.contrast: False vs fake: a false statement is not true; a fake Rolex is a copy made to fool you. Russian фальшивые деньги are counterfeit or fake money, not false money.

entries.meaning: Faltering has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The tax cuts were meant to boost the faltering economy.
The coach tried to save his faltering career.
She took a few faltering steps.
He answered in faltering English.
In a faltering voice, she thanked the crowd.

senses.head: Weak or unsteady and likely to stop or fail
examples: The tax cuts were meant to boost the faltering economy.
The coach tried to save his faltering career.
She took a few faltering steps.

senses.head: Of speech: hesitant and full of pauses
examples: He answered in faltering English.
In a faltering voice, she thanked the crowd.

entries.position: attributive only — after be it is usually the verb: The economy is faltering

entries.meaning: Famous — used mostly in writing. ---
examples: We ate at the famed diner on Main Street.
The town is famed for its maple syrup.
She studied under the famed architect Frank Gehry.
entries.takes: for + noun: famed for its beaches

entries.meaning: Relating to a family, or passed down through families. ---
examples: The disease has a strong familial link.
She felt a strong sense of familial duty.
The study looked at familial patterns of heart disease.
entries.contrast: Formal and medical; in everyday speech use family before a noun: family ties, family history. Don't confuse it with familiar (знакомый).

entries.meaning: Extremely hungry — informal. ---
examples: I'm famished — let's get something to eat.
The kids came home from practice famished.
A couple of famished hikers wandered into the diner.
entries.position: both — usually after a verb: I'm famished
entries.comparison: not gradable — an extreme adjective: absolutely famished

entries.meaning: Extremely enthusiastic about something, often too much. ---
examples: He's fanatical about keeping his car clean.
The band has a fanatical following.
She became even more fanatical about fitness after college.

entries.meaning: Fanciful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The idea that we'll finish by Friday is a little fanciful.
His story sounded fanciful, but it was true.
The gates were covered in fanciful ironwork.
The book has fanciful drawings of dragons and castles.

senses.head: Based on imagination rather than facts; not realistic
examples: The idea that we'll finish by Friday is a little fanciful.
His story sounded fanciful, but it was true.

senses.head: Decorated in an unusual, imaginative way
examples: The gates were covered in fanciful ironwork.
The book has fanciful drawings of dragons and castles.

entries.meaning: Fancy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: They took us to a fancy restaurant downtown.
We stayed at the fanciest hotel in town.
Don't get too dressed up — it's not a fancy party.
The cake had fancy decorations on top.
I just want a plain T-shirt, nothing fancy.
You don't need a fancy camera to take good photos.
The coach doesn't like fancy moves — just pass the ball.
He uses a lot of fancy words to sound smart.

senses.head: Expensive and stylish, for rich or important people
examples: They took us to a fancy restaurant downtown.
We stayed at the fanciest hotel in town.
Don't get too dressed up — it's not a fancy party.

senses.head: Decorated; not plain
examples: The cake had fancy decorations on top.
I just want a plain T-shirt, nothing fancy.

senses.head: Complicated, clever or technically advanced
examples: You don't need a fancy camera to take good photos.
The coach doesn't like fancy moves — just pass the ball.
He uses a lot of fancy words to sound smart.

entries.contrast: Only the adjective is common in American English; I fancy you (I like you) and Fancy a drink? are British. Nothing fancy means simple and ordinary.

entries.meaning: Strange and imaginary, like something from a dream or a fairy tale. ---
examples: The film is set in a fantastical world of talking animals.
Her paintings are full of fantastical creatures.
The costumes were even more fantastical than the sets.
entries.contrast: In everyday speech fantastic usually means 'wonderful'; fantastical keeps the older meaning 'strange and imaginary'.

entries.meaning: Holding political views at the extreme left end of the scale. ---
examples: The party expelled its far-left wing.
Her economics professor is far left.
Far-left and far-right groups both showed up that day.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: a far-left group
entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (a far-left candidate), two words after a verb (Her views are far left). The far left is a noun — the people themselves.

entries.meaning: Far-flung has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's traveled to far-flung places like Mongolia and Chile.
The company has offices in far-flung corners of the world.
My family is so far-flung that we rarely all meet.
The empire was huge and far-flung.

senses.head: Very far away
examples: She's traveled to far-flung places like Mongolia and Chile.
The company has offices in far-flung corners of the world.

senses.head: Spread out over a large area
examples: My family is so far-flung that we rarely all meet.
The empire was huge and far-flung.

entries.form: compound — far + flung, past participle of fling

entries.meaning: Holding very extreme left-wing political views. ---
examples: The far-left candidate won only 3 percent of the vote.
Some voters see his views as far-left.
The protest was organized by several far-left groups.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: far-left groups
entries.contrast: The far left, with no hyphen, is the noun: the people with the most extreme left-wing views.

entries.meaning: Distant in space or time. ---
examples: The story takes place in a far-off land.
We could hear far-off thunder.
Retirement still seems like a far-off dream.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb use far off or far away: The day is not far off

entries.meaning: Holding very extreme right-wing political views. ---
examples: The far-right party gained seats in parliament.
Critics called the website far-right.
Police are watching several far-right groups.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: far-right parties
entries.contrast: The far right, with no hyphen, is the noun: the people with the most extreme right-wing views.

entries.meaning: Faraway has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She dreamed of faraway places.
We could see the lights of a faraway town.
He had a faraway look in his eyes.
She answered in a faraway voice.

senses.head: Distant
examples: She dreamed of faraway places.
We could see the lights of a faraway town.

senses.head: Of a look or voice: dreamy, as if thinking about something else
examples: He had a faraway look in his eyes.
She answered in a faraway voice.

entries.position: attributive only — after a verb use two words: The town is far away

entries.meaning: So badly organized or silly that it is ridiculous. ---
examples: The trial was a farcical waste of time.
The meeting became farcical when nobody could find the agenda.
Each excuse was more farcical than the last.

entries.meaning: Very unlikely to be true or to happen. ---
examples: His excuse sounded pretty farfetched.
The plot of the movie is farfetched but fun.
It's not as farfetched as it sounds.
entries.form: compound — far + fetched; also spelled far-fetched

entries.meaning: Farsighted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm farsighted, so I need glasses to read.
Many people become farsighted after forty.
Buying land there in the 1970s was a farsighted decision.
The city's farsighted leaders built the subway early.

senses.head: Able to see things far away clearly, but not things close to you
examples: I'm farsighted, so I need glasses to read.
Many people become farsighted after forty.

senses.head: Thinking carefully about the future and planning for it
examples: Buying land there in the 1970s was a farsighted decision.
The city's farsighted leaders built the subway early.

entries.contrast: In American English the eye words are farsighted (дальнозоркий) and nearsighted (близорукий); British English says long-sighted and short-sighted.

entries.meaning: Fascist has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Mussolini led Italy's fascist government.
The group was banned for spreading fascist ideas.
My old boss was totally fascist about the dress code.
Protesters called the new law fascist.

senses.head: Relating to fascism: rule by a dictator, with extreme nationalism and no opposition allowed
examples: Mussolini led Italy's fascist government.
The group was banned for spreading fascist ideas.

senses.head: Very controlling and intolerant — used as an insult
examples: My old boss was totally fascist about the dress code.
Protesters called the new law fascist.

entries.comparison: more/most — mostly in the insulting sense: more fascist
entries.contrast: Fascist is the general word for this kind of politics; Nazi is specific to Hitler's Germany. A fascist is also a noun.

entries.meaning: Popular at a particular time, or used by people who follow the latest style. ---
examples: She always wears fashionable clothes.
They live in a fashionable neighborhood in Brooklyn.
Small weddings have become more fashionable lately.

entries.meaning: Fast has 4 distinct senses.
examples: He drives a really fast car.
She's the fastest runner on the team.
The fast lane is on the left.
He's a fast learner.
The internet here is much faster than at home.
We need a fast decision.
My watch is five minutes fast.
The clock in the car is fast, so don't panic.
The two girls became fast friends at camp.
Wash it in cold water — the dye isn't fast.

senses.head: Moving or able to move at high speed
examples: He drives a really fast car.
She's the fastest runner on the team.
The fast lane is on the left.

senses.head: Doing something or happening in a short time
examples: He's a fast learner.
The internet here is much faster than at home.
We need a fast decision.

senses.head: Of a clock or watch: showing a time later than the real time
examples: My watch is five minutes fast.
The clock in the car is fast, so don't panic.

senses.head: Firm and lasting — in fast friends, and of dye that does not wash out
examples: The two girls became fast friends at camp.
Wash it in cold water — the dye isn't fast.

entries.position: both — in the 'clock' sense only after a verb: My watch is fast; in fast friends only before a noun
entries.contrast: Fast is also the adverb: drive fast, never fastly. Fast is mostly about speed (a fast car); quick is about taking a short time (a quick question), though they often overlap. In fast asleep it means 'firmly', and the verb to fast means to go without food.

entries.meaning: Sleeping deeply. ---
examples: By nine o'clock the kids were fast asleep.
I found him fast asleep on the couch.
She was fast asleep before the movie ended.
entries.position: predicative only — The baby is fast asleep, not a fast asleep baby
entries.contrast: Here fast does not mean 'quick': fast asleep means sleeping deeply, not falling asleep quickly.

entries.meaning: Growing or getting bigger quickly. ---
examples: Austin is one of the fastest-growing cities in the country.
Bamboo is a fast-growing plant.
The company is small but fast-growing.

entries.meaning: Happening or moving quickly, with a lot going on. ---
examples: She works in a fast-paced newsroom.
The movie is fast-paced and full of action.
Life in New York is faster-paced than in Ohio.

entries.meaning: Very careful about details, cleanliness or order, sometimes too careful. ---
examples: He's fastidious about keeping his desk clean.
The restaurant is run by a fastidious chef.
When it comes to grammar, she's more fastidious than anyone I know.

entries.meaning: Containing no fat. ---
examples: I'll have a fat-free latte, please.
This yogurt is fat-free but full of sugar.
The store only sells fat-free milk.
entries.contrast: Fat-free means with no fat at all; low-fat means with a little. Fat-free food can still be high in sugar and calories.

entries.meaning: Fatal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There was a fatal accident on the highway last night.
The disease is almost always fatal.
He suffered a fatal heart attack.
Trusting him was a fatal mistake.
The plan has one fatal flaw.
The scandal proved fatal to her campaign.

senses.head: Causing death
examples: There was a fatal accident on the highway last night.
The disease is almost always fatal.
He suffered a fatal heart attack.

senses.head: Causing failure or very bad results
examples: Trusting him was a fatal mistake.
The plan has one fatal flaw.
The scandal proved fatal to her campaign.

entries.takes: to + person or thing: fatal to her campaign
entries.contrast: Russian фатальный often means 'fateful' or 'inevitable'; English fatal means 'causing death' or 'causing ruin'. A fatal accident is one in which someone died. For 'deciding the future', use fateful.

entries.meaning: Believing that events are decided by fate and cannot be changed. ---
examples: He's fatalistic about his health — he says what will be will be.
She has a very fatalistic view of politics.
Older voters were more fatalistic about the economy.

entries.meaning: Certain to happen or to do something, as if fate has decided it. ---
examples: Their marriage seemed fated to fail from the start.
Do you think we were fated to meet?
The novel tells the story of two fated lovers.
entries.position: both — usually after a verb with a to-infinitive: fated to fail

entries.meaning: Having an important, often bad, effect on the future. ---
examples: On that fateful morning, she decided to take the train.
It was a fateful decision that changed his life.
The fateful meeting took place in 1962.
entries.position: both — usually before a noun: that fateful day
entries.contrast: Fateful means having a very important, often bad, effect on the future; fatal means causing death or ruin. A fateful decision changed everything; a fatal decision led to disaster.

entries.meaning: Without a father, because he has died or is not part of the child's life. ---
examples: She grew up fatherless after her dad died in the war.
The charity helps fatherless children.
Millions of kids are growing up fatherless.

entries.meaning: Very tired — formal. ---
examples: Patients may feel fatigued for several weeks.
The fatigued soldiers slept wherever they could.
I felt more fatigued after the second dose.
entries.contrast: Fatigued is formal or medical; in conversation say tired or exhausted.

entries.meaning: Likely to make you gain weight. ---
examples: I love fries, but they're so fattening.
Try to avoid fattening snacks late at night.
Is beer more fattening than wine?
entries.form: -ing from fatten — what causes weight gain

entries.meaning: Fatty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Cut down on fatty foods like burgers and fries.
This cut of meat is fattier than chicken breast.
The soup was too fatty for me.
Doctors found fatty deposits in his arteries.
Omega-3 is a type of fatty acid.

senses.head: Containing a lot of fat
examples: Cut down on fatty foods like burgers and fries.
This cut of meat is fattier than chicken breast.
The soup was too fatty for me.

senses.head: Made of fat or relating to fat in the body — in medicine and science
examples: Doctors found fatty deposits in his arteries.
Omega-3 is a type of fatty acid.

entries.contrast: Fatty describes food and body tissue; a person is fat or, more politely, overweight. As a noun, fatty is a rude name for a fat person.

entries.meaning: Without any mistakes; perfect. ---
examples: Her English is faultless.
The pianist gave a faultless performance.
His driving record is faultless.

entries.meaning: Faulty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The fire was caused by faulty wiring.
The company recalled thousands of faulty airbags.
If the charger is faulty, the store will replace it.
The study was based on faulty data.
That's faulty logic.

senses.head: Not working correctly, or not made correctly
examples: The fire was caused by faulty wiring.
The company recalled thousands of faulty airbags.
If the charger is faulty, the store will replace it.

senses.head: Of reasoning or information: containing mistakes
examples: The study was based on faulty data.
That's faulty logic.

entries.meaning: Giving up something morally important in exchange for power, money or success. ---
examples: He made a Faustian bargain with the donors who paid for his campaign.
Taking the money was a Faustian deal she later regretted.
The novel explores the Faustian temptations of fame.
entries.form: -ian from Faust, the man in the legend who sold his soul to the devil
entries.contrast: Almost always in a Faustian bargain or a Faustian deal: giving up your values or your future for power, money or success now. Always with a capital F.

entries.meaning: Faux has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She bought a faux fur coat.
The chairs are covered in faux leather.
The kitchen has faux marble countertops.
He answered with faux innocence.
She let out a gasp of faux surprise.

senses.head: Made to look like a real material; artificial
examples: She bought a faux fur coat.
The chairs are covered in faux leather.
The kitchen has faux marble countertops.

senses.head: Pretended; not sincere — often humorous
examples: He answered with faux innocence.
She let out a gasp of faux surprise.

entries.contrast: Pronounced FOH: the x is silent, as in French. In stores faux is the polite word, so faux leather sounds better than fake leather.

entries.meaning: Favorable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The movie got favorable reviews.
Most voters have a favorable opinion of her.
The board was favorable to the idea.
Conditions are favorable for the launch.
We got a loan on favorable terms.
Interest rates are more favorable now than last year.

senses.head: Showing approval; positive
examples: The movie got favorable reviews.
Most voters have a favorable opinion of her.
The board was favorable to the idea.

senses.head: Good for someone or something; likely to help success
examples: Conditions are favorable for the launch.
We got a loan on favorable terms.
Interest rates are more favorable now than last year.

entries.takes: to or toward + an idea or person (approving of it); for + what it helps

entries.meaning: Favored has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Bikes are the favored way to get around campus.
It's a favored vacation spot for wealthy New Yorkers.
This was the most favored option in the survey.
The Lakers are heavily favored to win tonight.
She's the favored candidate in the race.

senses.head: Preferred; liked more than others
examples: Bikes are the favored way to get around campus.
It's a favored vacation spot for wealthy New Yorkers.
This was the most favored option in the survey.

senses.head: Expected to win
examples: The Lakers are heavily favored to win tonight.
She's the favored candidate in the race.

entries.takes: to-infinitive in the 'expected to win' sense: favored to win

entries.meaning: Liked more than all others of the same kind. ---
examples: What's your favorite movie?
Pizza is my favorite food.
We went back to our favorite restaurant for our anniversary.
entries.position: attributive only — my favorite song; after a verb it is the noun: This one is my favorite
entries.comparison: not gradable — most favorite is heard but avoided in careful English
entries.contrast: Favorite already means 'liked most', so my most favorite is redundant. In sports, the favorite (a noun) is the team or player expected to win.

entries.meaning: Praising someone too much in order to win their approval. ---
examples: The singer was surrounded by fawning fans.
The article was a fawning profile of the CEO.
Critics said the interview was far too fawning.
entries.form: -ing from the verb fawn (over someone), to flatter
entries.contrast: The verb fawn has nothing to do with a fawn, a baby deer (оленёнок).

entries.meaning: Worried, confused or upset by something — usually with not. ---
examples: She wasn't fazed by the tough questions.
The pilot didn't seem fazed at all.
The kids weren't fazed by the long drive.
entries.contrast: Almost always with a negative: not fazed, didn't seem fazed. It sounds the same as phased (phased out), which is a different word.

entries.meaning: Afraid, or worried that something bad will happen. ---
examples: Many residents are fearful of another flood.
The dog gave a fearful look and ran away.
Parents are more fearful for their kids' safety than they used to be.
entries.takes: of + noun or -ing; that-clause; for + the person you are worried about
entries.contrast: Fearful is more formal than afraid or scared and describes the person who feels fear; fearsome describes what causes it.

entries.meaning: Not afraid of anything. ---
examples: She's a fearless reporter who will ask anyone anything.
Little kids can be totally fearless around water.
He grew more fearless with every climb.

entries.meaning: Frightening, or so powerful that people are afraid of it. ---
examples: The team has a fearsome defense.
The grizzly bear is a fearsome animal.
The storm looked fearsome on the radar.

entries.meaning: Possible to do and likely to work. ---
examples: Is it feasible to finish the project by June?
We need a feasible plan, not a dream.
Solar power is becoming more feasible every year.
entries.takes: to-infinitive, usually in it is feasible to

entries.meaning: Feathered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Some dinosaurs were feathered.
She wore a feathered hat to the Kentucky Derby.
Our feathered friends need extra food in winter.
Feathered hair was hugely popular in the 1970s.
He still has the feathered haircut he had in high school.

senses.head: Having or covered with feathers
examples: Some dinosaurs were feathered.
She wore a feathered hat to the Kentucky Derby.
Our feathered friends need extra food in winter.

senses.head: Of hair: cut in soft layers that are brushed back from the face
examples: Feathered hair was hugely popular in the 1970s.
He still has the feathered haircut he had in high school.

entries.meaning: Soft, light or thin, like a feather. ---
examples: Dill has feathery green leaves.
Feathery clouds drifted across the sky.
The snow was light and feathery.

entries.meaning: Given special attention as an important part of an event, show or page. ---
examples: Tonight's featured speaker is the governor.
Check out the featured products on our home page.
The album's featured artists include several big names.

entries.meaning: Relating to feces, the solid waste from the body — medical and technical. ---
examples: The beach was closed because of fecal bacteria in the water.
The doctor ordered a fecal test.
Fecal matter can contaminate drinking water.

entries.meaning: Lacking the ability, effort or will to do anything useful; irresponsible. ---
examples: Her feckless brother keeps asking to borrow money.
Critics called the city council feckless.
The leadership has never looked more feckless.

entries.meaning: Annoyed and tired of something that has gone on too long. ---
examples: I'm fed up with this traffic.
Voters are fed up with both parties.
She finally got fed up and quit.
entries.русский: сытый по горло, доведённый до предела
entries.position: predicative only — I'm fed up, not a fed up person
entries.comparison: more/most — more fed up, most fed up
entries.contrast: Americans say fed up with; fed up of is heard in British speech but is avoided in careful English.

entries.meaning: Federal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Kidnapping is a federal crime.
He works for a federal agency in Washington.
Federal taxes are due in April.
The United States and Germany both have federal systems of government.
Canada is a federal country with ten provinces.

senses.head: Of the US national government, not the government of a state
examples: Kidnapping is a federal crime.
He works for a federal agency in Washington.
Federal taxes are due in April.

senses.head: Of a country or system: made of states or regions that share power with a central government
examples: The United States and Germany both have federal systems of government.
Canada is a federal country with ten provinces.

entries.contrast: In the US, federal means the national government in Washington, as opposed to the state governments: federal taxes vs state taxes, a federal crime. Russian федеративное государство is a federal state.

entries.meaning: Feeble has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her grandmother was too feeble to walk alone.
He spoke in a feeble voice.
That's a feeble excuse.
The team made a feeble attempt to come back.
That was the feeblest joke I've ever heard.

senses.head: Physically very weak
examples: Her grandmother was too feeble to walk alone.
He spoke in a feeble voice.

senses.head: Not effective or convincing
examples: That's a feeble excuse.
The team made a feeble attempt to come back.
That was the feeblest joke I've ever heard.

entries.meaning: Pretended; not real. ---
examples: She listened with feigned interest.
He looked up in feigned surprise.
Her feigned indifference didn't fool anyone.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: FAYND.

entries.meaning: Full of energy and determination, and ready to argue or fight — often said with approval. ---
examples: My feisty 90-year-old grandma still argues with everyone.
The little dog is feistier than the big one.
She gave a feisty speech against the plan.

entries.meaning: Feline has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Feline diseases spread quickly in shelters.
Lions and tigers are feline predators.
She moved with feline grace.
His eyes had a feline look.

senses.head: Relating to cats or the cat family
examples: Feline diseases spread quickly in shelters.
Lions and tigers are feline predators.

senses.head: Like a cat, especially graceful, quiet or sly
examples: She moved with feline grace.
His eyes had a feline look.

entries.contrast: A feline is also a noun, meaning a cat.

entries.meaning: Female has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Only female mosquitoes bite.
The company has only two female executives.
Is your kitten male or female?
You need a cable with a female connector on one end.
Screw the pipe into the female fitting.

senses.head: Belonging to the sex that can have babies or lay eggs
examples: Only female mosquitoes bite.
The company has only two female executives.
Is your kitten male or female?

senses.head: Of a plug or part: with a hole that another part fits into
examples: You need a cable with a female connector on one end.
Screw the pipe into the female fitting.

entries.contrast: Female is about sex, used for animals, forms and statistics (female workers, a female cat); feminine describes qualities traditionally linked to women. As a noun, a female for a woman sounds clinical or rude, so say a woman.

entries.meaning: Feminine has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She likes soft, feminine colors like pink and lavender.
The dress is very feminine.
Her new haircut looks more feminine.
In Spanish, casa is a feminine noun.
Russian adjectives change their endings to agree with feminine nouns.

senses.head: Having qualities traditionally thought typical of women
examples: She likes soft, feminine colors like pink and lavender.
The dress is very feminine.
Her new haircut looks more feminine.

senses.head: In grammar: belonging to the gender class that includes most words for women
examples: In Spanish, casa is a feminine noun.

entries.meaning: Saying honestly and directly what you think. ---

The old city is fortified with thick stone walls.
Most breakfast cereals are fortified with iron.
Port is a fortified wine.
Buy milk that is fortified with vitamin D.

senses.head: Protected by walls or other defenses against attack
examples: The soldiers held a fortified position on the hill.
The old city is fortified with thick stone walls.

senses.head: Having something added to make it healthier or stronger
examples: Most breakfast cereals are fortified with iron.
Port is a fortified wine.
Buy milk that is fortified with vitamin D.

entries.meaning: Happening by chance, especially by a lucky chance. ---

A fortuitous phone call led to her first job.
The timing could not have been more fortuitous.
entries.contrast: Strictly it means 'by chance', but most Americans now use it to mean 'lucky' as well, and the two meanings usually overlap.

entries.meaning: Lucky, or having good things that other people do not have. ---

It's fortunate that nobody was hurt.
We should help people who are less fortunate than we are.

senses.head: Moving or directed toward the front or ahead
examples: The team made little forward progress in the second half.
Lean your body into a slightly forward position.
A forward pass is legal in football but not in rugby.

senses.head: At or near the front of a ship, plane or vehicle
examples: Passengers in the forward cabin get off first.
The forward seats have more legroom.

senses.head: Too confident or friendly with someone you do not know well
examples: It was a little forward of him to ask for her number so soon.

She was more forward than the other girls in class.

entries.meaning: Planning for the future and open to new ideas. ---

The rock contains fossilized shells.

Teachers call mistakes that never go away fossilized errors.

The rock contains fossilized shells.

His ideas about women seem fossilized.
Teachers call mistakes that never go away fossilized errors.

She has a foul mouth when she's angry.

Police suspect foul play in his death.

entries.meaning: Four times as big or as many; or having four parts. ---

entries.meaning: Easily annoyed and hard to control, or always arguing. ---

examples: They ate a frugal dinner of beans and rice.
The monks lived on frugal meals.

entries.contrast: Of a person, frugal and thrifty are praise and cheap or stingy are criticism. economical is usually about things: an economical car.

entries.meaning: Producing good or useful results. ---
examples: We had a fruitful meeting with the investors.
The partnership has been fruitful for both companies.
This year's talks were more fruitful than last year's.

entries.meaning: Producing no useful result. ---
examples: After a fruitless search, they called the police.
Our efforts to reach him were fruitless.
She spent years on a fruitless attempt to get the case reopened.

entries.meaning: Tasting or smelling of fruit. ---
examples: This wine is light and fruity.
The candle has a sweet, fruity smell.
The red is fruitier than the white.
entries.contrast: fruity means tasting or smelling of fruit. Something made from fruit uses the noun fruit before the noun: fruit juice, fruit salad, not fruity juice.

entries.meaning: Wearing plain, old-fashioned clothes that make a person, usually a woman, look unattractive; of clothes, making someone look this way. ---
examples: She felt frumpy next to her stylish friends.
I don't want a frumpy sweater — show me something more modern.
That dress makes me look frumpier than my grandmother.

entries.meaning: Fucked-up has 3 distinct senses.
examples: That's a fucked-up thing to say to your sister.
The whole situation is fucked up.
He was pretty fucked up after the war.
She had a fucked-up childhood.
Everyone at the party was completely fucked up.
He got fucked up on cheap vodka.

senses.head: Vulgar slang: very bad, wrong, unfair or badly damaged
examples: That's a fucked-up thing to say to your sister.
The whole situation is fucked up.

senses.head: Vulgar slang: mentally or emotionally damaged
examples: He was pretty fucked up after the war.
She had a fucked-up childhood.

senses.head: Vulgar slang: very drunk or high on drugs
examples: Everyone at the party was completely fucked up.
He got fucked up on cheap vodka.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun, usually two words after a verb: it's fucked up
entries.form: compound — participle + particle, from the phrasal verb fuck up
entries.contrast: Vulgar slang and highly offensive — avoid it at work and with people you don't know. The polite version is messed-up.

entries.meaning: Vulgar slang: used before a noun to add strong emphasis, anger or annoyance. ---
examples: Where are my fucking keys?
This whole meeting is a fucking joke.
Turn off that fucking music!
entries.contrast: Vulgar and highly offensive. Before an adjective or adverb it is an adverb (fucking cold), not this adjective. Milder: freaking, damn.

entries.meaning: Happy and satisfied because you are doing something useful or using your abilities fully. ---
examples: She feels fulfilled in her work as a nurse.
He wanted a more fulfilled life than his father had.
Retirement left him bored and far from fulfilled.
entries.contrast: American spelling is fulfill, fulfilled, fulfillment; British spelling drops an l: fulfil, fulfilment.

entries.meaning: Full-blooded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The breeder sells full-blooded Arabian horses.
My grandfather was a full-blooded Italian and cooked like one.
The senator gave full-blooded support to the plan.
It was a loud, full-blooded rock performance.

senses.head: Of pure ancestry, with both parents from the same group or breed
examples: The breeder sells full-blooded Arabian horses.
My grandfather was a full-blooded Italian and cooked like one.

senses.head: Strong, enthusiastic and complete
examples: The senator gave full-blooded support to the plan.
It was a loud, full-blooded rock performance.

entries.comparison: not gradable — the 'wholehearted' sense takes more/most: more full-blooded

entries.meaning: Fully developed, with all the features of something. ---
examples: The argument turned into a full-blown fight.
Experts fear a full-blown recession.
Her cold turned into full-blown pneumonia.

entries.meaning: Of wine, coffee or a sound: rich and strong. ---
examples: Try a full-bodied red with the steak.
This coffee is dark and full-bodied.
The cello has a warmer, more full-bodied sound than the viola.

entries.meaning: Completely developed, or having reached full status. ---
examples: She's now a full-fledged attorney.
What started as a hobby became a full-fledged business.
The protest grew into a full-fledged movement.
entries.form: compound — full + fledged, from a bird with all its feathers grown
entries.contrast: American full-fledged; British writing says fully fledged.

entries.meaning: Having reached full adult size. ---
examples: A full-grown male can weigh 600 pounds.
The tree isn't full-grown yet.
She has three full-grown children.

entries.meaning: Full-length has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Their first full-length album comes out in May.
It's a full-length documentary, not a short.
There's a full-length mirror in the bedroom.
She wore a full-length gown.

senses.head: Of a movie, album or book: of the normal, complete length
examples: Their first full-length album comes out in May.
It's a full-length documentary, not a short.

senses.head: Reaching the whole height or length of something
examples: There's a full-length mirror in the bedroom.
She wore a full-length gown.

entries.русский: полнометражный; в полный рост, до пола

entries.meaning: Complete and not held back in any way. ---
examples: It wasn't a disagreement — it was a full-on argument.
They're in full-on panic mode.
He greeted me with a full-on bear hug.
entries.contrast: Informal. It is also an adverb meaning 'completely': She went full on into training.

entries.meaning: Filling a whole page. ---
examples: They took out a full-page ad in the Times.
The magazine ran a full-page photo of the crash.
Each chapter opens with a full-page illustration.

entries.meaning: Full-scale has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The country is on the edge of a full-scale war.
Police launched a full-scale investigation.
The museum has a full-scale replica of the shuttle.
They built a full-scale mock-up of the cockpit.

senses.head: As large or as complete as it can be
examples: The country is on the edge of a full-scale war.
Police launched a full-scale investigation.

senses.head: Of a model or drawing: the same size as the real thing
examples: The museum has a full-scale replica of the shuttle.
They built a full-scale mock-up of the cockpit.

entries.meaning: Of the normal, full size rather than a smaller version. ---
examples: We rented a full-size SUV.
The apartment has a full-size kitchen.
They sleep in a full-size bed.
entries.contrast: Also full-sized. Of a bed, full-size names a standard American size between a twin and a queen.

entries.meaning: Not weakened or diluted; at its full power. ---
examples: Take one full-strength tablet with food.
Full-strength coffee keeps me up all night.
The cleaner is too harsh if you use it full-strength.

entries.meaning: Born or carried for the whole normal length of a pregnancy. ---
examples: The baby was full-term and weighed eight pounds.
A full-term pregnancy lasts about forty weeks.
Full-term babies usually go home within a day.

entries.meaning: Loud and with no holding back, whether a sound or a show of support. ---
examples: He gave a full-throated defense of the policy.
The crowd let out a full-throated roar.
The senator offered full-throated support for the bill.

entries.meaning: Fulsome has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He thanked the host in fulsome terms.
The review's fulsome praise made me suspicious.
The senator promised a fulsome response to the questions.
Reporters asked for a more fulsome account of the meeting.

senses.head: So excessive that it sounds insincere
examples: He thanked the host in fulsome terms.
The review's fulsome praise made me suspicious.

senses.head: Full and generous — a newer use, common in the press
examples: The senator promised a fulsome response to the questions.
Reporters asked for a more fulsome account of the meeting.

entries.contrast: Traditionally an insult: fulsome praise is so thick that it sounds fake. Many Americans now use it simply to mean full or thorough, and careful readers still object.

entries.meaning: Enjoyable; giving pleasure. ---
examples: We had a fun weekend at the lake.
She's a fun person to work with.
Skiing turned out to be more fun than I expected.
entries.contrast: fun means you enjoy it; funny means it makes you laugh. a fun movie is entertaining, a funny movie is a comedy. fun is also a noun (We had a lot of fun), and funner/funnest are children's forms.

entries.meaning: Full of enjoyable activities. ---
examples: The resort promises a fun-filled weekend.
They spent a fun-filled afternoon at the fair.
It was three fun-filled days of music and food.

entries.meaning: Enjoying parties, jokes and good times. ---
examples: He's a fun-loving guy who never takes things too seriously.
They're a fun-loving family.
Her fun-loving side comes out on vacation.

entries.meaning: Functional has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Only one of the elevators is functional.
The kitchen is small but fully functional.
The furniture is plain and functional.
It's a functional building, not a beautiful one.
The new layout is more functional than the old one.
There's no functional difference between the two models.
The scan showed no functional damage.

senses.head: Working, and able to be used
examples: Only one of the elevators is functional.
The kitchen is small but fully functional.

senses.head: Designed to be practical rather than attractive
examples: The furniture is plain and functional.
It's a functional building, not a beautiful one.
The new layout is more functional than the old one.

senses.head: Relating to the way something works
examples: There's no functional difference between the two models.
The scan showed no functional damage.

entries.contrast: A dysfunctional family is not one that fails to work in this sense — dysfunctional means unhealthy relationships.

entries.meaning: Able to read a little, but not well enough to handle everyday forms, signs and instructions. ---
examples: About a tenth of the adults tested were functionally illiterate.
He hid for years that he was functionally illiterate.
The program helps functionally illiterate adults fill out job forms.

entries.meaning: Working as it should. ---
examples: It's the only functioning hospital in the region.
They want a functioning government, not a caretaker.
A fully functioning immune system clears the virus in days.
entries.comparison: not gradable — but fully functioning, high-functioning
entries.contrast: In The machine is functioning this is the verb, not the adjective.

entries.meaning: Forming the base of something, and therefore the most important. ---
examples: There's a fundamental difference between the two plans.
Free speech is fundamental to a democracy.
The problem is more fundamental than a software bug.
entries.contrast: The noun the fundamentals means the basics: the fundamentals of accounting.

entries.meaning: Following the strictest, most literal form of a religion or belief. ---
examples: He was raised in a fundamentalist church.
The party has taken a fundamentalist line.
Her reading of the text is strictly fundamentalist.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: He was raised by fundamentalists.

entries.meaning: Paid for with money provided for the purpose. ---
examples: The program is funded by the state.
She works in a well-funded research lab.
Is the project fully funded yet?
entries.comparison: not gradable — but well funded, underfunded

entries.meaning: Slow, dark and gloomy, the way a funeral is. ---
examples: The party had a strangely funereal mood.
He gave the news in a funereal tone.
The music was slow and funereal.
entries.contrast: funeral is the noun and the word you use before a noun (a funeral home); funereal means gloomy, like a funeral.

entries.meaning: Caused by or consisting of fungus. ---
examples: She's being treated for a fungal infection.
Fungal growth ruined the crop.
It's a fungal disease that spreads in wet weather.

entries.meaning: Able to be exchanged for another unit of exactly the same kind. ---
examples: Money is fungible — one dollar is as good as another.
These parts are fungible, so any supplier will do.
Fungible goods can be replaced one for one.
entries.contrast: A law and finance word, familiar to most people from non-fungible token.

entries.meaning: Funky has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She wears funky glasses.
It's a funky little coffee shop on Third.
The place got funkier after the new owners took over.
The band has a funky bass line.
I love the funky stuff they recorded in the seventies.
Something in the fridge smells funky.
His gym bag is seriously funky.

senses.head: Unusual and stylish in a relaxed, offbeat way
examples: She wears funky glasses.
It's a funky little coffee shop on Third.
The place got funkier after the new owners took over.

senses.head: Of music: with a strong, danceable rhythm
examples: The band has a funky bass line.
I love the funky stuff they recorded in the seventies.

senses.head: Smelling bad
examples: Something in the fridge smells funky.
His gym bag is seriously funky.

entries.meaning: Having fur on the inside for warmth. ---
examples: She pulled on her fur-lined boots.
He wore a parka with a fur-lined hood.
The gloves are fur-lined.

entries.meaning: Supplied with furniture. ---
examples: We're renting a furnished apartment near campus.
The place comes fully furnished.
Is the room furnished, or do we bring a bed?
entries.comparison: not gradable — but fully furnished, partly furnished
entries.contrast: furnished means it has furniture. The furniture itself is the furnishings.

entries.meaning: Furrowed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His furrowed brow told me the news was bad.
Her face was furrowed from years in the sun.
We walked across the furrowed field.
The furrowed ground was ready for seed.

senses.head: Marked with deep lines or wrinkles
examples: His furrowed brow told me the news was bad.
Her face was furrowed from years in the sun.

senses.head: Cut into long grooves, as a plowed field is
examples: We walked across the furrowed field.
The furrowed ground was ready for seed.

entries.meaning: Covered with fur, or soft like fur. ---
examples: A furry little dog ran up to us.
The blanket is soft and furry.
Her cat gets furrier every winter.

entries.meaning: Done quietly and secretly, so that nobody notices. ---
examples: He took a furtive glance at his phone.
They exchanged furtive looks across the table.
There was something furtive about the way she left.

entries.meaning: Fussy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He's fussy about what he eats.
Don't be so fussy — it's just a sandwich.
She's fussier than her sister about grammar.
The baby's fussy tonight.
He gets fussy around bedtime.
The wallpaper is a little fussy for my taste.
The dress is pretty, but the lace is fussy.

senses.head: Hard to please, and worried about small details
examples: He's fussy about what he eats.
Don't be so fussy — it's just a sandwich.
She's fussier than her sister about grammar.

senses.head: Of a baby: crying and unsettled
examples: The baby's fussy tonight.
He gets fussy around bedtime.

senses.head: Of a design: crowded with too many small details
examples: The wallpaper is a little fussy for my taste.
The dress is pretty, but the lace is fussy.

entries.contrast: picky is the everyday American word for the first sense: a picky eater.

entries.meaning: Certain to fail, so not worth doing. ---
examples: It was a futile attempt to save the building.
Arguing with him is futile.
Every effort so far has proved futile.

entries.meaning: Happening or existing at a later time. ---
examples: We are setting money aside for future expenses.
Future students will use the new library.
He introduced her as his future wife.
entries.contrast: Also a common noun (the future). As an adjective it goes only before a noun: future plans, never the plans are future.

entries.meaning: Looking as if it belongs to the future. ---
examples: The car has a futuristic dashboard.
The building looks futuristic against the old skyline.
Their designs are more futuristic than practical.

entries.meaning: Fuzzy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He gave her a fuzzy teddy bear.
The peaches were warm and fuzzy.
The photo came out fuzzy.
My memory of that night is fuzzy.
The rules get fuzzier the more you read them.

senses.head: Covered with short soft hairs
examples: He gave her a fuzzy teddy bear.
The peaches were warm and fuzzy.

senses.head: Not clear or sharp, whether a picture, a memory or a rule
examples: The photo came out fuzzy.
My memory of that night is fuzzy.
The rules get fuzzier the more you read them.

entries.contrast: warm and fuzzy is a fixed phrase for a comfortable, sentimental feeling: The ad gave me a warm and fuzzy feeling.
